title: Maggie's Library
author: Simon Pollard
summary: Simon Pollard draws on a podcast interview with space scientist Dame Maggie Aderin-Pocock to argue that a love of reading grows through a village of people around a child, not through a reading scheme. Maggie was stuck on Red Book One and was written off as nice but dim, and only recently learned she is dyslexic. What rescued her reading life was a television serial of Heidi, a father who took her to bookshops and libraries, a sister who retold stories, and the plain fact that someone believed in her. Pollard links this to his earlier posts on Developmental Language Disorder and on book ownership, warning that difficulty is easily mistaken for disinterest and that lowered expectations write a child's story for them. He closes with a practical step: 90 children at a local literary festival each received a dedicated copy of a new book to start their own library. The piece is a short, humane case for reading for pleasure, access to books and high expectations.
points: The story comes before the skill: Maggie's love of reading began with a dubbed TV version of Heidi, not with the graded reading scheme she was stuck on.
A child who finds reading hard is easily read as a child who cannot or will not learn, and an undiagnosed difficulty such as dyslexia or DLD can hide behind that misreading.
Lowering expectations because of where a child comes from or how they arrived risks writing that child's story for them.
Reading life is sustained by a village: a father with a torch and batteries, a sister retelling stories, libraries and book clubs that are open to everyone.
Giving children a book of their own, dedicated to them, is a concrete way to start the library that ownership and belonging depend on.
quotes: What changed things for Maggie wasn’t a reading scheme. It was a badly dubbed TV serialisation of Heidi. She loved the story so much that she found the book, probably at her local library, and read it for herself.

The story came before the skill. That’s exactly what we heard at the Open University’s Reading for Pleasure conference: a love of reading doesn’t come from doing everything “right”. It grows through connection.

A child who found reading hard was read as a child who couldn’t, or wouldn’t, learn. At school, she says, she used to pretend to fall asleep because she just wasn’t engaged. Every time we lower our expectations of a child because of where they come from, or how they arrived at our door, we risk writing their story for them.
Her father, who had dreamed of studying medicine, took her to Foyles bookshop on Charing Cross Road. To Maggie, it was “almost like a pilgrimage”.

At her 13th school, her records had been “scattered to the four winds”, and she was asked which stream she was usually in. She had always been in the bottom stream. This time, she told them she should be in the top one. They believed her, and she worked to prove them right.
You do need someone to believe in you,” Maggie said. For her, that was her father. “It might take you longer,” he told her, “but it doesn’t mean you can’t get there.
Whenever Maggie’s father bought a book, he wrote in the front in green ink. When she was 14 or 15, he gave her The Wind in the Willows, and inside it he wrote “Maggie’s library”.
But I keep thinking about Maggie at the Puffin Book Club, being told she shouldn’t get a book this time. For some children, a book of their own is never a given.
